top_choice_rationale: Cărtărescu is my first choice because his project (memory, the body and dream built into a sustained, densely patterned inner cosmos) is recognizable as a voice found 'in this writer's work and nowhere else', and it can be followed across decades and across poetry and prose. This is a judgment about the coherence and legibility of the whole oeuvre, not a claim that his invention is greater than Carson's. Carson is a close second: the round-2 exchange persuaded me that her recurring practice of reshaping inherited forms to carry grief and desire is a real unifying principle, and a citation limited to original verse narrative, elegy and essay reduces the delimitation problem. The margin is narrow. My judgment rests on public knowledge and translations, not independent verification. I cannot assess the Romanian prose at sentence level, and whether his late work extends or repeats the earlier project is unverified. The same later-work question applies to Carson. I rank both candidates above no award because both meet the common criteria of voice, formal achievement, depth and sustained quality, and the will's 'idealistic direction' read as seriousness of purpose does not separate them.
